hints: Look at 1-bromobutane as both a halogenoalkane and an alkane chain, so think about what the C-Br bond can do and what the C-H bonds can do.
Remember that a primary bromoalkane gives an alkene with hot ethanolic NaOH and an alcohol with aqueous NaOH, so statements 1 and 2 are both familiar.
Ask yourself if UV light with bromine can still replace a C-H hydrogen even when a Br is already present elsewhere in the molecule.
walkthrough:
**Identify the molecule**

Think of 1-bromobutane as $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$. It has a polar $\text{C-Br}$ bond that can break heterolytically, and it also has many $\text{C-H}$ bonds that can break homolytically.

**Check elimination**

With hot ethanolic NaOH, the $\text{C-Br}$ bond and a $\text{C-H}$ bond on the adjacent carbon break to form a double bond.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{NaOH(ethanolic)} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH=CH}_2 + \text{NaBr} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
So statement 1 is correct.

**Check hydrolysis**

With aqueous NaOH, warmed, $\text{OH}^-$ acts as a nucleophile and replaces Br by nucleophilic substitution. This is hydrolysis to an alcohol.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{NaOH(aq)} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{NaBr}$$
So statement 2 is correct.

**Check free radical substitution**

The carbon chain still contains $\text{C-H}$ bonds just like butane. With $\text{Br}_2$ and UV light, homolytic substitution can occur:

$$\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br} + \text{Br}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{UV}} \text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{Br}_2 + \text{HBr}$$
The existing Br does not stop this. It just gives a dibromo product. So statement 3 is correct.

**Combine the conclusion**

Since 1, 2 and 3 are all possible, the correct combination is 1, 2 and 3.

options.A: Correct. Elimination to but-1-ene, hydrolysis to butan-1-ol, and free radical bromination of the C-H bonds to give dibromobutanes are all possible for 1-bromobutane.
options.B: Incorrect. This combination includes only 1 and 2. Students choose this because they remember the halogenoalkane reactions well but wrongly think free radical substitution only happens with alkanes, forgetting the alkyl chain in 1-bromobutane can still react with Br2 under UV light.
options.C: Incorrect. This combination includes only 2 and 3. Students choose this if they forget that primary halogenoalkanes also undergo dehydrohalogenation with ethanolic NaOH to form an alkene.
options.D: Incorrect. This combination includes only 1. Students choose this if they confuse hydrolysis conditions or think only one reaction type is possible at a time, rather than different reagents giving different products.
